passage:
Ezra: Could we swap a couple of the soda options for sparkling water? A bunch of people asked for it in the survey.
Bianca: Great, let's just ban snacks entirely and hand out celery sticks at the door.
Ezra: I said a couple of sodas, Bianca.
cue: let's just ban snacks entirely and hand out celery sticks at the door
explanation: Ezra suggests swapping a couple of sodas, and Bianca mocks a far more extreme plan he never proposed. Her joke doesn't address the actual, modest request.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Bianca stays on the topic of the kitchen; she just inflates Ezra's suggestion into something easy to ridicule.

passage: Saw a physio post that runners should add two short strength sessions a week to cut injury risk. Sorry, but I'm not giving up running to become a gym rat. Some of us actually like being outside. Ten miles along the river this morning and it was glorious.
cue: I'm not giving up running to become a gym rat
explanation: The physio suggested adding two short strength sessions, not quitting running. Kay rejects a far bigger change than the one proposed, so the actual advice goes unanswered.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: Kay's main move isn't limiting the choices to two; it's arguing against a version of the advice the physio never gave.

title: Re: Proposed in-office days
passage: Hi Sandra, thanks for laying out the plan for two office days a week for teams that collaborate daily. I agree onboarding has been harder remotely, and our new hires have said as much. But if leadership's position is that remote employees can't be trusted and need to be watched, I think that's a real step backward for this team. Happy to talk it through. Malik
cue: remote employees can't be trusted and need to be watched
explanation: Sandra proposed two office days for teams that collaborate daily. Malik agrees about onboarding, then argues against a claim about distrust and surveillance that her plan never made.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Malik stays on the in-office plan; the problem is that he recasts its reasoning as distrust, which is easier to oppose.

passage: We all want children safe. I have two grandkids at Ridgeview myself. But the proposal before us, a 20 mph limit near schools during school hours, would essentially have every driver in Halverton crawling along at 20 all day, every day. That's not a safety plan; that's a traffic jam.
cue: every driver in Halverton crawling along at 20 all day, every day
explanation: Councillor Pruitt describes the proposal accurately, then attacks a much broader version: a citywide, all-day limit. The real plan covers school zones during school hours only.

whyNot.fal_false_dichotomy: He doesn't claim there are only two choices; he exaggerates the scope of the actual proposal so it's easier to dismiss.

title: Moving, but too sweeping
passage: In 'The Quiet Hour', Dr. Ilse Moss argues that heavy recreational scrolling after 9 p.m. is linked to poorer sleep in teens. The interviews are moving and she writes beautifully. But her view that screens are simply bad for kids ignores how many teens use them for homework, coding and staying close to friends. A more careful book would have been stronger.
cue: her view that screens are simply bad for kids
explanation: Odette summarizes the book's narrow claim about late-night scrolling, then criticizes a much broader 'screens are bad' view. Homework and coding don't touch the claim Moss actually made.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Homework and coding are on topic; the flaw is that Odette critiques a broader position than the one she just described.

title: Swap some city lawns for native plants, researchers urge
passage: A Pellham Institute study recommends converting 20% of city-owned lawns in parks and medians to native plantings, which it estimates would cut municipal irrigation by 15%. Landscaping association head Rob Kessler pushed back Monday, saying residents 'shouldn't be told to tear out the yards their kids play in.'
cue: shouldn't be told to tear out the yards their kids play in
explanation: The study is about city-owned lawns in parks and medians, but Rob responds as if it targeted families' backyards. He argues against a proposal nobody made.

whyNot.fal_red_herring: Rob stays on lawns and plantings; he shifts the target from city land to family yards, which misrepresents the study.

passage:
Luis: I think we should only take clients with budgets over $20k from now on.
Yasmin: Just so I've got it right: no projects under $20k at all? Last year 9 of our 14 projects were under that, and they covered most of summer payroll. So that rule would have cut most of our income in our slowest season.
Luis: Hm. Fair.
cue: Just so I've got it right: no projects under $20k at all?
explanation: Yasmin checks that her summary matches Luis's proposal before responding, then tests it against last year's actual projects. She argues against what he really said.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Yasmin restates Luis's rule accurately and confirms it, so her objection targets his real position, not a distorted one.

source: Business association chair Halina Varga · Main Street parking forum
passage: Mr. Brandauer's letter says, and I'm quoting, 'the new parking meters will hurt small shops on Main Street.' That's a fair worry. But when Oak Street added meters last year, shop revenue rose 6%, because spaces turned over instead of being taken all day by commuters. Main Street has the same commuter problem, so I expect meters to help our shops too.
cue: Mr. Brandauer's letter says, and I'm quoting,
explanation: Halina quotes Mr. Brandauer's exact objection and answers that version with evidence from a comparable street. She engages his real argument, not a weaker one.

whyNot.fal_straw_man: Halina quotes Mr. Brandauer word for word and answers that exact claim, so nothing has been distorted.
